front.title: Signed Digest Manifests for Multicast Datagram Authentication

abstract.t: This document defines a format for authenticating UDP datagrams delivered over IP multicast without changing them. The sender computes a digest over every data datagram of a flow, places the digests of up to 37 datagrams in a fixed-layout record, signs the record with Ed25519 under a prefix that names the flow, and sends it in band, on the flow's own source, group and port, immediately before the datagrams it covers, followed by a byte-identical twin. Every record begins with four fixed octets, and no data datagram does, so a receiver tells records from data by those octets alone. A receiver verifies one signature per record, hashes each datagram once, and delivers a datagram only after its digest matches an entry of a verified record; it needs no return channel. A well-known document supplies a flow's keys and parameters. A Media over QUIC profile and a browser profile use the format.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Multicast UDP delivery lacks the integrity protection that QUIC provides on unicast paths. A receiver of an IP multicast flow, whether joined natively, reached through an Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) relay or running in a browser, has no per-receiver connection over which the sender could authenticate what it sends: multicast transports are unidirectional ( Section 2.1), and a host that can inject into the path injects into every receiver at once. A format that authenticates each datagram before any use of it, costs the receiver one hash per datagram and a fraction of one signature verification, and asks nothing of the receiver but that it receive, serves every such receiver.

Asymmetric Manifest Based Integrity (AMBI) authenticates multicast packets with manifests of packet digests: a receiver holds packets and digests until the two meet and consumes a digest on admission (its Section 3.2). AMBI requires an authenticating transport for its manifests (its Section 4.1), and the three it defines (its Sections 4.2 to 4.4) are unicast; its Section 2.1.1 envisions a protocol that signs manifests and carries them over a multicast transport, leaving that to another specification. This document is that specification. The AMBI manifest of its Section 3.3 carries no signature, and its type-length-value (TLV) space (its Section 3.3.1.6) is extensible; this document defines a separate signed record rather than an AMBI TLV, so that the record is a fixed layout, verified before any parsing and carried on the flow's own (S, G, port), and restates the digest pseudoheader of AMBI Section 3.4.2 by value, since that document has expired. Discovery Of Restconf Metadata for Source-specific multicast (DORMS) discovers the metadata of an (S, G) through DNS and RESTCONF and, in its Sections 2.3.5 and 4.5, gates it per web origin with Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS); the well-known document of carries the same grant from the source address itself, and a DORMS record remains one way to deliver the same parameters. The threat model is that of : its integrity baseline (Section 2.3), injection rule (Section 2.7.2) and cross-origin authorization (Section 2.7.3) are met by construction, and what its Section 2.8.1 asks of a multicast protocol in place of a referrer check, that a client can unilaterally reject multicast data delivered for objects referenced by pages the server has not authorized, the well-known document's grant to a named origin delivers (, ).

This document defines the digest (), the manifest record and its signature (), what a sender emits and when (), what a receiver keeps and checks (), the parameters a flow's metadata declares and a well-known document that carries them (), an optional per-datagram trailer scheme for low-rate flows (), and the registry of scheme identifiers and the registration of the well-known URI (). It leaves to a profile how a receiver obtains the metadata (the well-known document, a DORMS record, an application catalog or provisioning), how the 32-octet ctx field of the record is derived from the application context, if at all (), and whether records reach a receiver by any path other than the flow's own port ().

A receiver that implements this document enforces it: there is no verify-and-report mode, and no datagram of a protected flow reaches an application except through the receiver rules of the scheme its metadata names, those of for manifest-ed25519-2 and of for ed25519-trailer-1.

Section 7.2 profiles this format for Media over QUIC (MoQ) as "bc-provenance" version 2: it derives ctx from the MoQ catalog, mirrors records on a MoQ track as a second path and carries flows in broadcasts, and it restates the format by value, so that the two documents agree on every wire-format fact and every rule of this document. A browser profile, proposed for the web platform under the title "Multicast Receive for Secure Contexts", names the format manifest-ed25519-2, scheme 1 of , fetches the well-known document on a page's behalf and delivers to the page nothing that has not admitted; lists the rules it adds.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

All multi-octet integers are unsigned and big-endian; u8, u16, u32 and u64 are unsigned integers of that width; a string is its UTF-8 octets; H is the function selected by the record's hash_alg (), with a 32-octet output. Test vectors are in .
SSM: Source-Specific Multicast .
AMT: Automatic Multicast Tunneling .
TESLA: Timed Efficient Stream Loss-Tolerant Authentication .
ASM: Any-Source Multicast, the service model of Section 1 in which any host may send to G; the sender of an ASM flow is the declared senderAddress of its metadata ().

Flow: every datagram the sender emits to one (S, G, port), S being the source address, G the group address and port the UDP destination port, that the flow's metadata declares protected (), other than the records it emits there. A sender that carries the same content on two (S, G, port) tuples has two flows.
Data datagram: a datagram of a flow; no data datagram of a flow using manifest-ed25519-2 begins with the ASCII octets "MHM2" ().
Record: one UDP datagram on the flow's port that carries the digests of one window, signed (). "Manifest record" and "record" are the same thing.
Window: a contiguous run of at most 37 data datagrams of a flow whose digests one record carries.
Twin: the byte-identical second copy of a record ().
Path: a route by which records reach a receiver. This document defines one, in band on the flow's port; a profile MAY add others ().
Epoch: a 32-bit counter carried in every record that increments on sender restart and key change (); counters and replay floors are kept per epoch.
Generation: the life of a flow under one streamId (); a change of streamId resets receiver state ().
Key set: the keys the flow's metadata names for it, each a (kid, publicKey, firstEpoch) triple ().
Sender: the entity that emits the flow and signs its records. "Sending entity" names the same entity wherever this document uses it.
Receiver: an implementation of . It may act for an application, for a web page on whose behalf it joins, or for a decoder it feeds.
Metadata: the parameters of that a receiver holds for a flow, however obtained: from the well-known document, a DORMS record, an application catalog or out-of-band provisioning.
Context source: whatever a profile derives the record's ctx from (); a receiver "holds the context source" when it can recompute ctx.
Profile: a specification that binds this format to an application by fixing how the metadata is delivered, how ctx is derived and which record paths exist.

section.name: Overview
section.t: Data datagrams are untouched: no header, no trailer and no parsing are added to them. Their authenticity comes from signed records that the sender interleaves with them on the flow's own (S, G, port); every record begins with the four octets "MHM2", and no data datagram does. For each protected flow the sender computes a digest over every data datagram the flow emits, Forward Error Correction (FEC) repair symbols included where a flow carries them; collects digests into windows of at most 37 datagrams or manifestTimerMs, whichever closes first; places each window in a fixed-layout manifest record; signs the record with a dedicated Ed25519 key under a network-identity prefix; and emits the record on the flow's port immediately before the datagrams it covers, followed by a second copy. Receivers verify one signature per window, hash each datagram once, and admit a datagram to delivery only after its digest matches an entry of a verified manifest.

The digest pseudoheader, the hold queue and the consume-on-admission rule are those of AMBI ( Sections 3.4.2 and 3.2); the signed record is a multicast-carried manifest delivery of the kind that AMBI Section 2.1.1 leaves to another specification, and this document carries it in band, on the flow's own (S, G, port).
The digest algorithm is carried in the signed record as a Named Information Suite ID (); SHA-256 is mandatory to implement.

A receiver delivers an admitted datagram's payload as received, and it knows the datagram's sequence and the epoch of the record that listed it (), which it MAY make available to the application, sequence only together with that epoch. It delivers nothing else of a protected flow except, where its profile says so (the browser profile does, ), an admitted datagram's arrival time and the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) field of its IP header ; no digest covers either (), so an on-path party can delay the datagram or change that field without failing its digest, and a party that can send as S () sets both for a datagram whose copy it gets to the receiver in time to be the one admitted, as steps 1 and 2 of let it do for a carousel repeat and for a datagram it receives sooner than the receiver does, the sender's copy then being dropped as already admitted. Every flow parameter that enters the pseudoheader or the signature prefix is declared in the flow's metadata; the record carries none of them, and names only the digest function (hash_alg) it uses and the key (kid) of the metadata's key set that verifies it, so a receiver that holds the metadata needs no other state to start, and nothing read from a datagram but its length enters the pseudoheader.

This document defines two schemes and registers an identifier for each (). Scheme 1, manifest-ed25519-2, is the manifest format of through and is mandatory to implement. Scheme 2, ed25519-trailer-1 (), signs each datagram in a trailer and suits low-rate flows; a receiver MAY implement it. A flow's metadata names the scheme the flow uses.

section.name: Digest
section.t: Every data datagram the sender emits in a protected flow has a digest; a record has none:

payload is the entire UDP payload as transmitted, any FEC payload identifier or trailer the application appends included, so a verified digest also authenticates whatever the datagram carries about its place in a repair block. This document authenticates received datagrams: what a receiver reconstructs from admitted datagrams alone is admitted with them, and what it reconstructs with the help of anything else is outside this document.
pseudoheader is the AMBI pseudoheader of Section 3.4.2, restated here by value since that draft has expired:
section.artwork: pseudoheader = S # 4 octets (IPv4) or 16 octets (IPv6) || G # 4 or 16 octets, same family as S || 0x00 # zeroes || 0x11 # protocol, UDP || u16(payload_length) # length of payload in octets || u16(src_port) || u16(dst_port) || u32(streamId)
section.t: It is 20 octets with IPv4 addresses and 44 with IPv6; streamId occupies AMBI's Manifest Stream Identifier field. Addresses are in native width, never IPv4-mapped. S is the address from which the sending entity transmits the flow: the source address of an SSM flow, and the declared senderAddress of an ASM flow (). src_port and dst_port are both the flow's port: the sender MUST emit every datagram of the flow with port as its UDP source port. streamId is the flow's streamId (). Every input is declared in the flow's metadata or provisioned with it (), so a receiver forms the pseudoheader without reading anything from the datagram but its length, and one digest verifies the same bytes whatever carrier delivers the datagram. A carrier that re-addresses the flow or its records, or carries the datagrams in any other form, is not covered: the pseudoheader binds S, G and the ports, and a record verifies as it was signed or not at all.

section.name: Hash Algorithms
section.t: hash_alg is a Suite ID of the IANA Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry ( Section 9.4), a value from 0 to 63; values 64 to 255 are not Suite IDs and MUST NOT be sent. Only a suite whose output is 256 bits is usable, since every digest field is 32 octets; the truncated suites MUST NOT be used. Suite 1, sha-256 , is mandatory to implement. A receiver MAY implement other 256-bit suites; it drops a record whose hash_alg it does not implement (). All records of one flow carry the same hash_alg for the life of a flow generation (streamId, ); a change of algorithm is a new generation.

section.name: Manifest Record
section.t: A manifest record is one UDP datagram that the sender emits on the protected flow's own (S, G, port), with port as its UDP source port; its first four octets, "MHM2", tell it apart from the flow's data datagrams (). Every field except the signature is at a fixed offset, and the signature is the last 64 octets.

tr.td: epoch, increments on sender restart and key change
mseq, manifest counter, monotonic per (flow, kid, epoch)
sent, emission time in POSIX seconds (below)

section.t: Length is 132 + 32 x count octets, 164 to 1316. The cap of 37 digests is an MTU choice: a record and every header it acquires on the way travel as one unfragmented datagram on a 1500-octet path. At 37 digests the record is 1316 octets: 1344 on the wire with IPv4 and UDP headers and 1364 with IPv6, and 1394 or 1414 once an AMT relay adds its own IPv4 or IPv6 header, UDP header and 2-octet Multicast Data header around the IPv6 datagram. That leaves 86 to 106 octets for one further tunnel or extension header on the path; an IPv4 record through an IPv4 relay is 1374 octets, leaving 126. A record of 39 digests would still fit a 1500-octet path through AMT; one of 42 (1476 octets, 1504 under IPv4 and UDP) would not fit even without it, and neither leaves that room, whatever the address family of record or relay. Digest i of a record covers sequence = first_seq + i.

flags: bit 0, the least significant bit of the octet (mask 0x01), epoch end (); bits 1 to 7 reserved, MUST be zero on send and ignored on receipt. A sender SHOULD set bit 0 in the record of the last window of every epoch whose end it plans (a key change, a counter that would exceed 2^64 - 1 (), an orderly restart); an epoch that ends unplanned, as at a crash, has no such record.

sent is the sender's clock when the record is signed, truncated to whole seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z with leap seconds excluded, from a clock synchronized to UTC within 1 s; the twin of a record () carries the original's value. It is a count of seconds, not the 16.16 NTP short format, so it wraps in 2106 rather than every 18.2 hours. A sender whose clock is further off than the tolerance of makes its flow unverifiable to receivers that check freshness.
A record has no other repeat form: its second copy is a byte-identical twin ().

section.name: Signature Context Binding
section.t: The signature is computed over:
section.artwork: signed_message = "mcast-manifest-v2" || 0x00 # 18-octet label || u32(streamId) || S # 4 or 16 octets || G # 4 or 16 octets || u16(port) || record[0 .. len - 64)
section.t: with S, G, streamId and port as declared for the flow (, ), and the signature is the 64-octet Ed25519 signature of Section 5.1 (the PureEdDSA variant, with no prehash and an empty context) under the key that kid names. The prefix binds the flow's network identity; a receiver needs no state to check it beyond those four values, which it takes from the flow's metadata or its provisioning ().

ctx is 32 octets that a profile of this format MAY derive from the application context it binds the flow to, under a label of the profile's choosing and with the record's hash_alg ( Section 7.2.4 binds the MoQ catalog this way). A flow with no such profile sets ctx to 32 zero octets. A receiver that holds the context source recomputes ctx and MUST reject a record whose ctx differs (); any other receiver carries ctx blind. ctx is part of the signed message, not an Ed25519 context string, which the variant above does not carry.
A valid (record, datagrams) pair therefore cannot be replayed onto another flow, flow generation, key or epoch; sent bounds replay within an epoch to the clock tolerance of .

section.name: Keys, Epochs and Sequence Numbers
section.t: kid is an unsigned 32-bit integer carried in the clear in every record and names a key of the flow's key set (), each key signing the epochs from its firstEpoch up to, but not including, the next larger firstEpoch in the set. epoch never decreases under one kid: a sending entity MUST NOT reuse an epoch under a kid, across generations or restarts, and a generation that would start below the kid's last epoch starts under a new kid ().

The protected unit is a flow: every datagram the sender emits to one flow (S, G, port) that its metadata declares protected (), other than the records it emits there. A flow has one port, which no other flow of the same (S, G) shares and which carries its records (); its sequence counter (below) and its mseq counter () are kept per (kid, epoch). mseq starts at any value and increases by one for every window the flow closes under one (kid, epoch), in emission order, which the replay floor of (mseq + 64 <= highest_mseq) and the twin deadline of (before the signed record of window mseq + 64) assume.

sequence is a 64-bit counter the sender assigns per (flow, kid, epoch): it starts at any value and increases by one for every data datagram the flow emits, in emission order, repair symbols included. It is carried only in manifest records, never in data datagrams, and is unrelated to any sequence number the payload carries. Digest i of a record covers sequence = first_seq + i, so one window is a contiguous run of the flow. A datagram the sender emits twice (a carousel) has two sequences and two digests. An application MUST NOT assume that sequence continues across an epoch change. Neither counter wraps within an epoch: a sender ends the epoch (the record whose flags bit 0 is set, ) before either would exceed 2^64 - 1, and the comparisons this document states on them, mseq + 64 <= highest_mseq included, are integer comparisons that an implementation evaluates without unsigned underflow or overflow.

section.name: Sender Behavior
section.t: A sender emits a flow's records on the flow's port, interleaved with its data datagrams. It MUST NOT emit a data datagram whose first four octets are the ASCII octets "MHM2", since a receiver takes such a datagram for a record (). RTP , LCT (FLUTE and ROUTE ), NORM and MMTP version 0 packets cannot begin with those octets, because the version field they lead with excludes the octet 0x4D ("M"). A QUIC short header packet ( Section 17.3.1) can begin with 0x4D; a sender that protects a multicast QUIC channel ( Section 2) meets the rule above by giving it a Channel ID that neither begins with the octets 0x48 0x4D 0x32 ("HM2") nor is a prefix of them. An application that listens on port and does not implement this document receives the records and their twins as well; an implementation of one of those protocols reads each as a packet of another version: RTP version 1, LCT or NORM version 4, MMTP version 1.

A sender closes a window after 37 datagrams or after manifestTimerMs since the window opened, whichever comes first; the timer governs only while the flow emits at most 37 datagrams per manifestTimerMs (1850 per second at the default, about 21 Mbit/s of 1400-octet datagrams), and the count cap governs above that. A sender MUST NOT close more than 64 + V x t windows on one flow in any interval of t seconds, a long-run rate of at most V per second, where V = max(1000, 1.25 x maxBitrate / (8 x 512 x 37)) is computed from the flow's declared maxBitrate () and is the rate at which a receiver's verification budget refills (step 1 of ); 64 + V x t is the envelope of that bucket, whose depth of 64 the sender's bursts share with the network's jitter. At the count cap that is 37 x V datagrams per second, which above V's floor (a maxBitrate above about 121 Mbit/s) is 1.25 x maxBitrate of 512-octet datagrams: a flow at its declared rate stays under V while its datagrams average at least about 410 octets (V is 8,248 at 1 Gbit/s) and its windows close at the count cap, since a window the timer closes counts against V however few datagrams it covers. A sender above the ceiling starves its own receivers, whose budgets drop its records and expire its windows as loss (). A sender MAY raise manifestTimerMs to at most maxAuthDelayMs / 4 on low-rate flows; manifestTimerMs is at least 1 (), so the timer alone never closes more than 1000 windows per second.

The signed record MUST be transmitted immediately before the first datagram it covers (only the twin of an earlier window MAY come between them), so the sender holds at most one window of data: 20 ms below about 21 Mbit/s, where the timer closes windows at the default, 8.3 ms at 50 Mbit/s and 4.1 ms at 100 Mbit/s with 1400-octet datagrams. A twin, a byte-identical copy of the record, MUST be transmitted after the last datagram the record covers, no later than maxAuthDelayMs / 2 after the record and before the signed record of window mseq + 64, so that at most 63 later records precede it and it arrives above the replay floor of , however fast the flow closes windows; RECOMMENDED is to transmit it immediately after the signed record of window mseq + 2 and before the first datagram that record covers, or on its own at the maxAuthDelayMs / 2 deadline when window mseq + 2 has not closed by then. The two copies then bracket the window's datagrams: a contiguous loss burst that removes both copies has removed every datagram between them, and a datagram that survives such a burst has a usable copy on one side of it, whatever the flow's rate and timer; only two separate losses can leave an arriving datagram without a copy, and then at most 37 datagrams expire from the hold queue (). Every twin of an epoch MUST be transmitted before the first record of a later epoch, since a receiver drops the records of an earlier epoch once its grace period ends (); every twin of the epoch not yet transmitted when its last datagram has been sent, the twin of the record whose flags bit 0 is set included, follows that datagram at once. A receiver handles either copy by step 1 of and drops the second with one lookup and one hash.

At 37 digests per window, a record and its twin cost about 71 octets per 1400-octet datagram (5.1%); data datagrams are untouched. With the 20 ms timer the two copies cost about 5.6% at 10 Mbit/s, about 9% at 2.5 Mbit/s and about 23% at 128 kbit/s, where one 1400-octet datagram is emitted every 87.5 ms and, at the default maxAuthDelayMs, no timer within maxAuthDelayMs / 4 batches two; raising manifestTimerMs pays only where several datagrams fit in one timer period, and below that rate the trailer scheme of is the cheaper one. Manifest records MUST NOT be FEC-protected; the twin is their loss remedy.

The sender MUST write the current epoch to the flow's metadata as minEpoch at every epoch change, sender restart included, so that a joiner with current metadata cannot be fed an earlier epoch (); what a restart requires of the sender's epoch is in .

section.name: Receiver Behavior
section.t: A receiver that implements this format enforces it: a datagram of a protected flow is admitted only after its digest matches an entry of a verified record, and there is no verify-and-report mode. A receiver MUST be able to pin "authentication required" for a flow independently of its metadata. A receiver that fetches no metadata MUST be provisioned out of band with the keys, firstEpoch included, and minEpoch and, per protected flow, the streamId, S, G, port and maxBitrate the metadata would declare (), and any non-default maxAuthDelayMs and manifestTimerMs: the record carries none of them; keys are never taken from a carrier's signaling. A receiver that pins keys takes the key set, firstEpoch included, from the pin rather than from the metadata, and MUST keep with the pin, across sessions, the highest epoch it has verified under each pinned kid; in step 1 below it drops, at join, a record whose epoch is below that value for its kid, so metadata that carries a lower minEpoch cannot reopen an epoch a verified record has closed. The pin stores no value read from the metadata: every receiver takes minEpoch from the metadata it fetched, or provisions it with the keys, and it bounds that session only. A receiver with no pin is protected at its first join against an earlier epoch only as far as that metadata is. A receiver that implements no algorithm a flow's records carry verifies nothing on that flow: it admits nothing and treats the flow as one that yields no data.

Whether a flow is protected is a property of the flow's metadata, not of any datagram: a receiver that holds metadata declaring a flow protected delivers nothing from that flow except through the receiver rules of the scheme that metadata names, those of this section for manifest-ed25519-2 and of for ed25519-trailer-1.

section.name: Source and Destination Checks
section.t: On an ASM flow a receiver MUST discard, before any parsing or hashing, a datagram on port whose IP source address is not senderAddress; behind an AMT relay the address is that of the encapsulated header of the AMT Multicast Data message . On an SSM flow reached natively the network forwards the datagrams of every source of G that the receiver has joined, and flows of two sources in G may share a port (), so a receiver MUST discard, before any parsing or hashing, a datagram on port whose source address is not S; a receiver reached through an AMT gateway MUST discard it in the same way, since nothing upstream of its gateway filters the encapsulated source address and does not authenticate Multicast Data messages. A receiver MUST likewise discard, before any parsing or hashing, a datagram on port whose IP destination address, behind an AMT relay that of the encapsulated header, is not G, since flows of one S in different groups may share a port; a datagram that passes both checks belongs to the flow (S, G, port) with S as in .

section.name: State
section.t: State per flow: the current epoch with the kid that set it; the grace period that ends maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs after the current epoch became current and, until it ends, the previous epoch; the flow's hash_alg, fixed by its first verified record; per (kid, epoch) the verified mseq values above the replay floor, each with the hash_alg digest of the record's bytes, the highest_mseq that verified records have raised (step 1) and, once a verified record has flags bit 0 set, the mseq that closed it; the verification budget of step 1 with a count of the records it dropped; a pending table of (digest, sequence, expiry) entries, each with the epoch of the record that inserted it; the digests recorded as admitted, each until the time of recording plus maxAuthDelayMs; and a hold queue of (digest, datagram, expiry) entries in arrival order, digest being absent from an entry until the first record of the flow is verified (step 2). State per receiver: the time of the last metadata re-fetch that an unknown kid triggered (), shared by all the receiver's flows, and the per-kid epoch floor kept with a key pin, one for each key set the receiver pins and shared only by the flows that key set is attached to (), even where two key sets list the same keys, as two channels of one well-known document may.

maxBitrate, maxAuthDelayMs and manifestTimerMs size the hold queue and the pending table (steps 1 and 2), and maxBitrate the verification budget of step 1; a receiver bounds all three by local policy. At the budget of step 1 the pending table holds at most 37 x (64 + V/1000 x (maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs)) entries, 11,248 at the defaults up to a maxBitrate of about 121 Mbit/s and 75,610 at 1 Gbit/s, and the hold queue at most maxAuthDelayMs x maxBitrate / 8000 octets, 1.25 MB at 50 Mbit/s and the default maxAuthDelayMs.

section.name: Processing
section.t: A receiver applies the following, in this order, with no variable-length interpretation before a cryptographic check. A datagram on port whose first four octets are the ASCII octets "MHM2" is a record candidate and takes step 1; every other datagram on port is a data datagram and takes step 2. Nothing else is read to decide. A record candidate that fails a check of step 1 is dropped and counted as that step specifies, and it is never held, hashed as a data datagram or delivered.

li.t: Record datagram (on port, magic "MHM2"). Require 164 <= len <= 1316 and (len - 132) mod 32 == 0. Read the fixed-offset integers magic, kid, epoch, mseq, count, hash_alg and sent and the 32 octets of ctx. Drop before any cryptography if: magic differs; kid is not in the key set, or epoch is outside its range (); (kid, epoch, mseq) is already verified (this drops the second copy of a record with one lookup and one hash, a copy of the previous epoch arriving after its grace period included; a dropped copy whose bytes hash, under the flow's hash_alg, to the digest kept with the verified entry is the record itself, its twin or a replay of it, and one whose bytes do not match is not; on the single record path of this document neither moves any floor or timer, highest_mseq having been raised when the entry was verified, below, and the distinction serves only a profile that adds a path ()); epoch is below the current epoch and is not the previous epoch within its grace period (below), or, when no record has yet been verified, is below minEpoch or below the pinned floor for its kid; mseq + 64 <= highest_mseq(kid, epoch) (replay floor, none before a record of that (kid, epoch) has raised highest_mseq, no upper bound; the sum does not wrap, ); mseq is above the mseq that closed the epoch, once a verified record has closed it; sent is more than 7 s + maxAuthDelayMs behind, or more than 6 s ahead of, the receiver's UTC clock (freshness: the sender's 1 s bound and the receiver's 5 s bound, plus, behind, the truncation of sent to whole seconds and the delivery of the twin); count != (len - 132) / 32; hash_alg is not in the receiver's accepted set, or differs from the flow's hash_alg once one is fixed; or, on a receiver that holds the context source of , ctx differs from the value recomputed from it (any other receiver carries ctx blind). Charge the per-flow verification budget, a token bucket of depth 64 refilled at V tokens per second, V = max(1000, 1.25 x maxBitrate / (8 x 512 x 37)) from the flow's declared maxBitrate (): 1000 up to about 121 Mbit/s, 8,248 at 1 Gbit/s; drop and count a record that finds it empty (nothing before the signature tells a forged record from a genuine one, so a forged record spends the same token, ). Verify the Ed25519 signature over signed_message; drop on failure, and only on success read first_seq, flags and the digests, except that a profile MAY read first_seq with the fixed-offset integers above, only to drop, among the checks above, a record whose first_seq + count - 1 exceeds a bound the profile sets, as does. If epoch is above the current epoch, or this is the first verified record, make epoch current and make the former current epoch the previous epoch, with a grace period that ends maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs after now (the sender emitting every twin of it before the new epoch's first record, ), fix the flow's hash_alg from this record if none is fixed yet, and hash every held datagram that has no digest yet; pending entries and held datagrams of the previous epoch are not flushed and live out their expiry. A record of the previous epoch that passes the checks above is processed under that epoch's own floor and verified set and never changes the current epoch. Record (kid, epoch, mseq) as verified, with the hash_alg digest of its bytes, and raise highest_mseq. For each (digest, sequence) of the record, in order: if the hold queue holds a datagram with that digest, admit the oldest such datagram, remove it from the queue and record its digest as admitted until now + maxAuthDelayMs (step 2); otherwise insert the pair into the pending table with expiry now + maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs (240 ms at the defaults). Once every pair of the record is processed, drop from the hold queue each datagram still held whose digest is now recorded as admitted: it is a repeated copy of a datagram this record admitted, which step 2 would not have held after the admission; its drop is not an expiry and counts toward nothing (). A window's digests are inserted once: a record for a window already verified is dropped above, so no entry is refreshed or re-inserted. If flags bit 0 is set the epoch is closed at this mseq (): later records with this epoch and a higher mseq are dropped, pending entries live out their expiry, and the next epoch is accepted by the rule above.

Data datagram (any other datagram on port). Compute D with the flow's hash_alg (a datagram that arrives before the first record of the flow is verified is held without a digest) and look it up in the pending table, which maps a digest to its entries (carousels repeat byte-identical datagrams). Hit: remove the entry lowest in (epoch, sequence) order, admit the datagram and record D as admitted until now + maxAuthDelayMs. Miss: drop the datagram if D is so recorded (a copy of an admitted datagram delivered again is never held); otherwise append (D, datagram) to the hold queue with expiry now + maxAuthDelayMs, the queue bounded to maxAuthDelayMs x maxBitrate / 8000 octets, each held datagram counting its UDP payload plus its IP and UDP headers (28 octets on an IPv4 flow, 48 on an IPv6 one), so that empty or short datagrams hold no more entries than their octets on the wire pay for; drop the newest on overflow, since dropping the oldest would let an injector purge legitimately held datagrams, and drop at expiry, as unauthenticated. Repair symbols follow the same rule, so an injected symbol is dropped before it reaches a decoder. A receiver MUST NOT deliver to an application, or feed to a decoder, a datagram of a protected flow that it has not admitted under step 1 or 2, on whatever carrier it arrived.

section.t: Replay. Receivers in an explicitly configured digital video recorder (DVR) or replay mode MAY relax the epoch, floor and freshness checks. A (digest, sequence) entry is consumed when matched, so a replayed datagram finds no entry unless a legitimate identical copy is still pending, in which case the replay consumes that copy and the later legitimate copy is dropped (the application receives the same bytes either way, with the replay's arrival time and ECN field where its profile delivers them (); this is a denial of service only, bounded by the carousel repeat count). Cross-flow replay is excluded by streamId, S, G and port in both the digest and the signature.

section.name: Key Rotation and Re-fetch
section.t: A key change is an epoch change (). The sender adds the next kid to the metadata with the firstEpoch at which it will sign, at least one metadata lifetime ahead; signs with it from that epoch; and raises minEpoch. A receiver that holds that metadata accepts the retired kid below the successor's firstEpoch only, so records the retired key signs are admitted until the grace period for the new epoch ends (step 1 of ); a receiver that verifies no record of the new epoch keeps the epoch before it current, which the retired key still signs, and a receiver whose metadata or pin predates the rotation is exposed to the retired key until it re-fetches or is re-provisioned (). A record with an unknown kid triggers at most one metadata re-fetch per 30 s per receiver; until then such records are dropped. A receiver that pins the keys of the record's flow makes no such re-fetch, since no re-fetch changes a pinned key set. The browser profile does not re-fetch on an unknown kid: it drops such records and re-fetches the well-known document only when the metadata lifetime of expires, so an injected record cannot make it fetch on demand. Whenever a re-fetch or a re-provisioning changes the key set or a kid's range, the receiver re-applies the range check of to the (kid, epoch) that set each flow's current epoch; where it now fails, the receiver discards that flow's state as it does on a streamId change (), the digest of every held datagram included, and returns to the join state of step 1, so a record a retired key signed before the re-fetch cannot hold the flow afterwards. Revocation is key removal, effective within one metadata lifetime, reckoned from the removal as asks of a sender. The metadata lifetime is the lifetime that derives from the response's Cache-Control for a receiver that uses the well-known document, and whatever bounds the validity of a DORMS record, a catalog or a provisioning otherwise.

section.name: Generation Change
section.t: The per-flow state of belongs to the flow generation (): when the streamId the metadata, or a receiver's provisioning, declares for the flow changes, the receiver discards every per-flow item of but the verification budget and its count and the hold queue (the current and previous epoch, hash_alg, the per-(kid, epoch) mseq state, the pending table and the admitted digests), clears the digest of every held datagram, and processes the next record as the first of the flow under the join-time floors of step 1 of .

section.name: Additional Record Paths
section.t: This document delivers records only in band, on the flow's port, so the record that makes an epoch current is the first record of that epoch the receiver verifies, the grace period of the previous epoch starts at that moment, and one replay floor per (kid, epoch) suffices. A profile that adds a second record path (a unicast mirror of the same record octets, for instance) MUST specify, per path, the replay floor and the grace period a record arriving on that path meets, which records raise or start them, and a deadline after which no record of the previous epoch is admitted on any path, reckoned from the time the current epoch became current, since on such a profile a path can see the new epoch's records late or not at all; it MUST also specify which verification budget of step 1 a record arriving on each path charges, with the count of dropped records that goes with it, how a record verified on one path is treated when its copy arrives on the other, by how much the pending-entry expiry and the admitted-digest retention of step 1 are widened for a record on that path, so that the lead of one path over the other does not expire an entry before the datagrams it covers arrive, and by how much, if at all, the freshness tolerance of step 1 is widened for a record on that path, which admits at join windows that much older (). Section 7.2.7 does so for a MoQ manifest track: one budget per path, each with its count; the previous-epoch deadline at the bound of its Section 7.2.5 plus maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs after the current epoch became current; the pending expiry and the admitted-digest retention widened by the mirror's lead, the bound of that section until one is measured; and, on a receiver that widens its hold by W, at most 5 s, for a relay-buffered path, the freshness tolerance, and where no lead applies the pending expiry, of a record read from the manifest track widened by W as well. A profile that adds no path applies this document as written.

section.name: Clocks
section.t: The freshness check needs a receiver clock synchronized to UTC within 5 s. A receiver without one MAY skip that check alone; it then accepts any window of the current epoch at join and has no protection against replay of the epoch's earlier windows until its first verified record sets the floor (). Every other timer of this section (maxAuthDelayMs, manifestTimerMs and the expiries derived from them) is a local interval and needs no synchronized clock.

section.name: Cost
section.t: A datagram from another source, or to another destination than G, costs one or two address comparisons (); one that spoofs S and is addressed to G costs one four-octet comparison and, if it does not begin with "MHM2", one hash, two lookups and, on a miss of both, space in the hold queue until expiry, so a copy of an admitted datagram costs one hash and two lookups; one that begins with "MHM2" is an injected record, which costs at most one verification inside the budget or, with an unknown kid, no verification and at most one metadata re-fetch per 30 s (), a replayed one whose (kid, epoch, mseq) is still verified one lookup and one hash while its mseq is above the replay floor (the already-verified lookup of step 1 precedes the freshness check), one outside the verified set and outside the freshness tolerance that lookup alone, a miss, before the epoch floor, the replay floor or the freshness check drops it, the second copy of a verified record one lookup and one hash. With one verification per 37 datagrams, a Cortex-A53 without SHA2 instructions spends about 0.26 of a core at 100 Mbit/s and, under a record flood at V's floor of 1000 verifications per second, about 0.43 of a core on signature checks, the hashing of the flow's own datagrams continuing beside them; a core with SHA2 instructions hashes in a fraction of that time, and its signature checks do not depend on them. A record flood costs at most V verifications per second, so the flood figure rises with V: 8,248 per second, V at 1 Gbit/s, is 0.33 of a 3 GHz Zen 3 core and 1.84 Cortex-A76 cores at 1.5 GHz. The browser profile drops and counts, before hashing, a datagram whose UDP payload exceeds 1472 octets over IPv4 or 1452 octets over IPv6 (one unfragmented 1500-octet packet), so a datagram reassembled from fragments, up to about 64 KiB, cannot cost it about 45 times the hashing of a 1400-octet one.

section.name: Flow Metadata and the Well-Known Document
Flow Parameters
section.t: A receiver needs the following for each protected flow. They are delivered by any authenticated means a profile specifies: the well-known document of , a DORMS record or AMBI metadata , an application catalog ( Section 7.2.6), or out-of-band provisioning (). The names below are those of the well-known document; a profile that carries them under other names maps them one to one.

ul.li: scheme (REQUIRED): the name of the scheme the flow uses, manifest-ed25519-2 for this format and ed25519-trailer-1 for , from .

S (REQUIRED): the address from which the sending entity transmits the flow, S of . On an SSM flow it is the SSM source; on an ASM flow it is declared as senderAddress, which MUST NOT appear on an SSM flow. Two ASM flows whose senderAddress differ MAY share G and port; the source check of separates them.

G (REQUIRED): the group address, of the same address family as S. Wherever a receiver matches metadata to a flow it compares S and G as IP addresses, never as strings, and an address of one family never matches one of the other, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address being of the IPv6 family ().

port (REQUIRED): the UDP destination port of the data datagrams and of the records, twins included, and the source port from which the sender emits them all (, ). Two flows of the same (S, G) MUST NOT share a port, so that no port of an (S, G) carries the data or the records of two flows: metadata MUST declare each (S, G, port) at most once, and a receiver whose metadata declares one twice holds no parameters for that flow and MUST NOT join it ().
streamId (integer, REQUIRED): 32-bit value chosen per flow generation, bound into every digest and signature.

keys (array, REQUIRED): one to four {kid, publicKey, firstEpoch} objects. kid is an unsigned 32-bit integer carried in the clear in every record; publicKey is the 32-octet Ed25519 public key; firstEpoch is the first epoch the key signs. A key signs the epochs from its firstEpoch up to, but not including, the next larger firstEpoch in the array, and the key with the largest firstEpoch signs every later epoch. kid values MUST be unique within the key set and firstEpoch values MUST be distinct within the array. A receiver that takes its keys from metadata whose keys is absent or not an array, has no or more than four entries, has an entry that is not an object or that lacks a kid, publicKey or firstEpoch or has one of the wrong kind, repeats a kid or a firstEpoch, names a kid or firstEpoch outside its field width, or names a publicKey that is not 32 octets, holds no key set for the flow or flows that key set is attached to (below): it admits nothing from them, as it does on a flow whose records carry an algorithm it does not implement (), and the other flows of the same metadata, with key sets of their own, are unaffected; a receiver that pins keys is unaffected, since its key set comes from the pin. A receiver drops, before verification, a record whose epoch is outside its kid's range (), so a retired key cannot carry a receiver past its successor's firstEpoch.

minEpoch (integer, REQUIRED): the lowest epoch a receiver accepts at join (step 1 of ); after its first verified record the current epoch is the floor, with the previous epoch admitted until its grace period ends, maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs after the current epoch became current (step 1). The sender MUST write the current epoch at every epoch change, sender restart included, so a joiner with current metadata cannot be fed an earlier epoch.
maxAuthDelayMs (integer, OPTIONAL, default 200, range 50 to 1000): how long a receiver holds a datagram whose digest has not arrived.
manifestTimerMs (integer, OPTIONAL, default 20, at least 1): the window timer of .

maxBitrate (integer, REQUIRED): the sender's declared ceiling for the flow in bit/s, counting the UDP payloads of its data datagrams (IP and UDP headers and records excluded), which bounds the receiver's hold queue (step 2 of ) and sets the verification budget V of step 1 and the sender's window ceiling (). declares the same value as the endpoint's bandwidth.

section.t: The ranges above are binding. A receiver that finds maxAuthDelayMs outside 50 to 1000 or manifestTimerMs below 1 MUST either clamp it to the nearest bound or decline the flow, as its profile specifies, and MUST NOT use the out-of-range value. The other parameters are identifiers or sizes, not tunables, and a clamped identifier names a port, key, generation or epoch the sender never declared: a receiver that finds a port of 0, a maxBitrate that is not a positive integer, or port, streamId or minEpoch outside its field width, MUST decline the flow, and a keys array of no or more than four entries, or one naming a kid or firstEpoch outside its field width, yields no key set (keys above). The browser profile clamps maxAuthDelayMs (to 50 and 1000) and declines a flow whose manifestTimerMs is below 10, the floor of , or exceeds maxAuthDelayMs / 4 after that clamp (at most 250 ms), the ceiling sets for a raised timer, which the profile applies to the default of 20 as well, so its grace period never exceeds 1.5 s and its pending table never exceeds the bound of at maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs = 1500 ms.

maxAuthDelayMs, manifestTimerMs and maxBitrate are per flow. keys and minEpoch are per key set; the metadata attaches a key set to one flow (the well-known document carries one per channel, ) or to several ( Section 7.2.6 carries one per broadcast), and every flow it is attached to uses that key set and that minEpoch. A sender MUST keep every flow a key set is attached to at one epoch and change it on all of them together: that minEpoch, and the per-kid epoch floor that a receiver which pins keys keeps for that key set (), bound each of them at join, so the records of a flow left at a lower epoch than another are dropped at join. A flow using ed25519-trailer-1 declares scheme, S, G, port, keys and maxBitrate only.

A receiver keeps the parameters it holds for up to a metadata lifetime (), and a record whose kid it holds triggers no re-fetch. For one metadata lifetime after it publishes a new maxBitrate, maxAuthDelayMs or manifestTimerMs, a sender therefore keeps within the old value as well as the new one: it sends above the old maxBitrate only once that lifetime has passed. A receiver that holds the old streamId verifies no record of the new generation until it re-fetches, so a sender that changes streamId, as a move to another hash suite does (), first publishes, for at least one metadata lifetime, a lifetime no longer than the interruption it accepts.

section.name: The Well-Known Document
section.t: A sender that serves receivers which can fetch over HTTPS publishes its flows' parameters at

where <S> is the SSM source address as the IP address literal in the host of an https URI ( Section 4.3.5), IPv6 in brackets, never a host name; the well-known URI is registered in . The document is JSON , served with the media type application/json; the well-known URI is used with the https URI scheme only:

version (integer, REQUIRED): the document format; this document defines 1. A document whose version is not 1 is not used: a receiver treats it as listing no channel () and takes no parameter from it, so no flow is protected on its account. A receiver ignores a member it does not recognize at the document, channel, integrity and key level, so that a later revision of this document can add members under version 1 without disturbing a receiver that implements this one; version changes only when a receiver that implements this document would otherwise misread the new format.

channels (array, REQUIRED): one object per flow the source serves to such receivers. A document that is not a JSON object, or whose channels is not an array, lists no channel. Each carries source (S, an IP literal, equal to the address the document was fetched from), group (G), port, maxBitrate and an integrity object with scheme and, for manifest-ed25519-2, streamId, minEpoch, maxAuthDelayMs, manifestTimerMs and keys, each as defines it; publicKey is base64url-encoded without padding ( Section 5), 43 characters for the 32 octets. For ed25519-trailer-1 the integrity object carries scheme and keys only. A receiver matches a flow by (S, G, port) exactly, comparing source and group to S and G as IP addresses after parsing their textual forms, not as strings, since an IPv6 literal has several textual forms; source and group MUST be IP address literals in the IPv4address or IPv6address form of Section 3.2.2 (dotted-decimal with no leading zeros; IPv6 without brackets or a zone identifier), never names, of one address family, that of the address the document was fetched from, and a receiver ignores a channel whose address members are not; an IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal is of the IPv6 family and does not match an IPv4 address, the families themselves having to match. It ignores an element of channels that is not a JSON object, a channel it cannot match, every channel whose (S, G, port) another channel of the same document also declares, one whose port violates , one that lacks a member other than keys that this section or marks REQUIRED for its scheme, or carries a member of this section under a JSON value of a kind other than the one named here (a number with an integer value for port, kid, firstEpoch and each member this section or calls an integer, a string for source, group, scheme and publicKey, an object for integrity and for each element of keys, an array for keys), a member of the wrong kind being absent, so that a REQUIRED one other than keys leaves the channel ignored and an OPTIONAL one takes its default, one whose keys, at a receiver that takes its keys from the document, yields no key set (keys absent or not an array, an element of it that is not an object or lacks a kid, publicKey or firstEpoch, no or more than four entries, a repeated kid or firstEpoch, a kid or firstEpoch outside its field width, or a publicKey that is not 43 base64url characters decoding to 32 octets, ; a receiver that pins keys is unaffected, since its key set comes from the pin), and one whose scheme it does not implement; each of these is ignored alone, and the other channels of the document are unaffected. The document describes SSM flows only, since it is fetched from S; an ASM flow's metadata is delivered by other means. A receiver bounds the size of the document and the number of channels by local policy.

section.name: Fetching the Document
section.t: A receiver fetches the document with an HTTPS GET addressed to the IP literal S. The server's certificate MUST contain an iPAddress subjectAltName ( Section 4.2.1.6) carrying S in native width in network byte order, an IP-ID in the terms of Section 1.5, and the receiver MUST verify the certificate as an https client does for a host that is an IP literal ( Section 4.3.4), with S as its IP-ID reference identifier and an octet-for-octet match of S against that entry, no partial match ( Sections 6.2 and 6.4); no DNS record is a security boundary of this format, and a receiver never resolves a name to find the document. A receiver MUST NOT follow a redirect, and it sends no credentials.

A receiver that acts on behalf of a web origin sends that origin in the Origin request header, as the CORS protocol of does, and uses the response for that origin only if the response carries an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header naming that origin; a wildcard is not consent, nor is a response that carries no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header or one naming another origin or the string null, which names no origin, and such a receiver MUST treat each of them as listing no channel for its origin and MUST NOT use it for that origin. A receiver acting for an origin that serializes to null sends no Origin header and treats the response as listing no channel for it, and a sender MUST NOT send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null. A sender that publishes for every origin echoes the request's Origin, a null Origin excepted, which it answers as it answers a request that carries no Origin header, and sends Vary: Origin, as asks of any response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin is not a single static value, so that a cache, the receiver's own or one shared on the path to S, does not serve one origin's response, or the response to a request that carried no Origin header, to another origin. This is the per-origin gate that Sections 2.3.5 and 4.5 place on DORMS metadata, carried from a DNS-discovered server to the source address itself and with the wildcard rejected rather than discouraged; it is the CORS-like cross-origin authorization that Section 2.7.3 asks for. A receiver that acts for no origin sends no Origin header and ignores the response header.

A receiver keeps the parameters it took from the document for a metadata lifetime () derived from the response's Cache-Control and clamped to 60 s at least and 24 h at most: the value of the max-age directive ( Section 5.2.2.1) less the response's current age, reckoned as Section 4.2.3 of that document does from the Age and Date header fields and the receiver's own request and response times; Expires, s-maxage and heuristic freshness (its Sections 5.3, 5.2.2.10 and 4.2.2) are not consulted. A response with no Cache-Control, with no max-age or a max-age that is not a non-negative integer, or one that carries no-store or no-cache (its Sections 5.2.2.5 and 5.2.2.4), gives the minimum, 60 s. This lifetime governs the parameters the receiver holds, not the HTTP response: any HTTP cache the receiver's fetch passes through follows as usual, so a no-store response is not stored and a no-cache one is not reused without validation. A sender MUST give every response that carries the document either a max-age of at most 86400 with the must-revalidate directive ( Section 5.2.2.2) and with no s-maxage and no directive that lets a cache serve it stale (its Section 4.2.4), or no-cache, or no-store; so no cache holds the document fresh longer than its max-age or serves it stale, and a cache that cannot reach S answers with an error, a fetch that fails. A sender reckons each wait and bound that this document states in metadata lifetimes, from a change, as 60 s plus the longest max-age it gave a response for the document in the 24 h before that change: a cache can answer a receiver's first fetch with a copy stored before the change, and the receiver keeps what it took from that copy for 60 s at least. The receiver re-fetches the document when the lifetime it derived expires. That lifetime does not consult Expires, s-maxage or heuristic freshness and is clamped at 24 h, so a cache that stored the document can still hold it fresh when the lifetime ends; the receiver therefore does not reuse a stored response of its own for that re-fetch without validation and sends it with the request directive Cache-Control: no-cache ( Section 5.2.1.4), which asks a cache on the path to validate with S before reusing what it stored. Such a re-fetch that fails, or returns a response the receiver cannot use (one that does not verify as this section requires, is not the document of , carries a version the receiver does not implement, or carries no consent for its origin, as above), is treated as a document that lists no channel for the flow, since a receiver that kept the expired document would let an attacker that can block the fetch keep a withdrawn grant or a removed key in force past its lifetime; a flow whose channel or origin grant the re-fetched document no longer lists, or, at a receiver that takes its keys from the document, whose key set it no longer lists, is left (a key set that still names a key but drops the current kid is a key-set change under , not a withdrawal), so withdrawal of consent is effective within one metadata lifetime, reckoned from the withdrawal as above, and a sender that wants faster withdrawal publishes a short lifetime. A 304 (Not Modified) leaves in place each stored header field it does not carry, a stored Access-Control-Allow-Origin included ( Sections 3.2 and 4.3.4), so a sender that withdraws an origin's grant without changing the document also changes the validators it sends with the document for that origin (a new ETag, a later Last-Modified). A record with an unknown kid triggers at most one re-fetch per 30 s per receiver (). Such a re-fetch comes within the lifetime, when a cache that stored the document can still hold it fresh, so the receiver does not reuse a stored response of its own for it without validation and sends it with the request directive Cache-Control: no-cache ( Section 5.2.1.4), which asks a cache on the path to validate with S before reusing what it stored; a re-fetch so triggered that fails, or returns a response the receiver cannot use, leaves the parameters the receiver holds in force until their lifetime expires, since the records that triggered it are unauthenticated and are dropped either way, and treating that failure as a withdrawal would let any host that can inject one such record and keep the server's answer from the receiver make every receiver that re-fetches on such a record leave the flow at once.

section.name: Browser Profile
section.t: This section is informative. It collects what the browser profile of adds to this document, for its receivers and for the senders that serve them. Its rules on a record with an unknown kid (), on maxAuthDelayMs and manifestTimerMs (), on datagram size () and on ingress above its ceiling () are stated in those sections.

The browser profile gives the page, with each datagram it delivers, the datagram's arrival time and the ECN field of its IP header as received (on the AMT path, as its own AMT gateway leaves that field after decapsulation), the two values that lets a profile deliver and that no digest covers.

A sender whose flow serves the browser profile starts each sequence counter () below 2^53 and ends the epoch before first_seq + count - 1 would exceed 2^53 - 1, the largest integer n for which a JavaScript Number holds n and n + 1 exactly: the browser profile reads first_seq with the other fixed-offset integers of step 1 of and drops, before verification, a record past that bound, and the datagrams that record covers expire unadmitted.

A sender whose flow serves the browser profile keeps its datagrams averaging at least 512 octets at the declared maxBitrate, and its manifestTimerMs at 10 ms or more, because the browser profile derives its ingress ceiling for the flow from that rate, max(1000, 1.25 x (1 + 2/37) x maxBitrate / (8 x 512)) datagrams per second counted before verification (the 2/37 for a record and its twin per 37 data datagrams), and sheds datagrams above it (); a window the timer closes adds a record and its twin whatever its count, so a shorter timer can take a flow at its declared rate past that ceiling, and the browser profile declines a flow whose manifestTimerMs is below 10 (). V of is sized on the same 512 octets. Such a sender also keeps manifestTimerMs at or below maxAuthDelayMs / 4, the default included, since the browser profile declines a flow above that ceiling (): a sender that declares a maxAuthDelayMs below 80 also declares a manifestTimerMs from 10 to maxAuthDelayMs / 4.

The browser profile drops an IP fragment that arrives inside an AMT Multicast Data message and never reassembles one. An AMT relay adds 30 to 50 octets of encapsulation, and it fragments an IPv4 datagram too large for its tunnel when the datagram allows fragmentation and otherwise drops it, as it drops an IPv6 one ( Section 5.3.3.6). A sender that wants its flow to reach browser receivers through relays on 1500-octet paths therefore keeps the UDP payloads of its data datagrams at or below 1422 octets over IPv4 and 1402 over IPv6, which fit a relay of either address family.

The browser profile also bounds the hold queue of step 2 of at 16 MB (128 ms at 1 Gbit/s), dropping and counting held data past it, and joins flows within its ceilings on every device: 1 Gbit/s per flow, and 1 Gbit/s in total over the flows of all the pages and frames that one user permission covers; 50 Mbit/s per flow and 100 Mbit/s in total on a link the platform reports as metered. A user agent may lower these ceilings but never raise them, and it lowers them alike on every device, so that no ceiling tells a page about its device. It declines a flow whose maxBitrate exceeds the ceiling per flow or would take the sum of maxBitrate over the flows that permission covers past the total, and, when a link becomes metered, it leaves a flow whose maxBitrate is above the metered ceiling per flow, then each flow that the same check, rerun over the remaining flows in the order they joined, would decline. A lowering takes effect when the user agent next starts: it applies to the joins after that start and never reaches a flow already joined.

The browser profile's authenticated-rate breaker leaves a flow whose authenticated rate stays above 1.25 x maxBitrate for 5 s, counting the UDP payloads of the data datagrams it admits as maxBitrate counts them (), and its loss breaker leaves one that loses more than 25% of the datagrams its records list in each of three successive 5 s windows. The loss breaker counts as lost only listed digests that expire unmatched and the windows of records missing from the verified mseq sequence, never a held datagram that no verified record lists: injected data datagrams never count as lost, but a flood can still trip it, since genuine datagrams the ingress ceiling sheds, and windows whose records the verification budget dropped, count as lost. Silence trips neither breaker.

A browser-profile receiver that authenticates no datagram of a flow within 2 s of its native join, because no native delivery reaches it or none that reaches it verifies, looks up the AMTRELAY records in the reverse zone of S and, unless a proxy applies to the relay or the user agent's policy rules out non-proxied UDP, reaches the flow through its own AMT gateway until it leaves the flow, using only a relay that such a record, or a Relay Advertisement from such a relay, names, at a global unicast address and on UDP port 2268 ( Section 7.2). The relay is trusted for carriage alone: every datagram is verified as requires, with the source and destination checks of applied to the encapsulated header. The join itself discloses the subscription, apart from the fetch of : a native join puts (S, G) on the receiver's link and in its network's multicast routing state; the AMTRELAY lookup, made even where the receiver then stays native, shows S to the receiver's resolver, and to the path where DNS is not encrypted, and shows the receiver's resolver and the time of the lookup to the servers authoritative for the reverse zone of S; resolving a relay that a record gives by domain name, a name the holder of the reverse zone of S chooses, shows the receiver's resolver and the time of the fallback to the servers authoritative for that name; and a join through a relay shows the receiver's address and the (S, G) it receives, in the clear ( Section 6), to the relay, which the holder of the reverse zone of S chooses, directly or through a relay it names, and to any observer of the unicast AMT leg, for as long as the receiver stays joined. An injector that keeps the receiver from authenticating any datagram in the first 2 s of a native join, by a flood of the kind describes, can therefore force that lookup and, where a relay is found and nothing keeps the receiver native, that relay join. One such flood reaches every receiver below the point where it is injected, so it does so at every browser-profile receiver there that joins while it lasts, and each that moves to a relay draws its own unicast copy of the flow until it leaves the flow: a load on the relays that grows with the audience while the injector's cost does not, an amplification of the kind that Section 2.1 warns of, forced here by loss rather than by an invalidated object.

section.name: The ed25519-trailer-1 Scheme
section.t: A receiver MUST implement manifest-ed25519-2 and MAY implement ed25519-trailer-1, which a flow's metadata selects by its scheme (). The scheme signs each datagram and so costs a receiver one signature verification per datagram; it suits control and signaling flows of a few hundred datagrams per second where zero authentication latency matters more than CPU, and at 128 kbit/s of 1400-octet datagrams its overhead, 5.7%, is below that of the manifest format (). A receiver MAY refuse a flow that declares ed25519-trailer-1 with maxBitrate above 10 Mbit/s, since every injected datagram costs one full verification ( Section 7.1).
Each datagram of the flow ends in an 80-octet fixed-layout trailer:

tr.td: seq, sequence number, per (flow, kid, epoch)

section.t: The signature is the Ed25519 signature of Section 5.1, under the key that kid names, over
section.artwork: signed_message = S # 4 or 16 octets || G # 4 or 16 octets || u16(port) || u32(epoch) || u64(seq) || payload # the datagram without its trailer
section.t: with S, G and port as declared for the flow and addresses in native width as in . kid, the key set and the rules for epoch under a kid are those of and ; seq starts at any value and increases by one for every datagram the flow emits under the (kid, epoch).

A receiver applies the following, in this order. Require len >= 80. Read kid, epoch and seq at their fixed offsets; drop the datagram if kid is not in the key set or epoch is outside its range. Apply the replay window before any cryptography: the receiver keeps, per (flow, epoch), a sliding window of 1024 sequence numbers whose right edge is the highest verified seq; a seq below the left edge, or already seen inside the window, is dropped; a seq inside the window not yet seen, or above the right edge, proceeds to verification; on success a seq above the right edge becomes the new right edge, and one inside the window is marked seen, as in the anti-replay processing of Section 3.3.2. An epoch above the current one, once a datagram of it verifies, becomes current and resets the window; a datagram of a lower epoch is dropped. Verify the signature; drop on failure. Deliver the payload with the trailer removed, seq and epoch being the datagram's sequence and epoch for the application. The source and destination checks of apply to the datagrams of such a flow as to any other.

Key rotation and revocation are as in , with no grace period: the key set bounds each kid to its epoch range, and a re-fetch that changes the key set or a kid's range re-applies the range check to the (kid, epoch) that is current and, where it now fails, discards the flow's window and returns to the join state. The scheme carries no emission time and its metadata no minEpoch, so a receiver that joins accepts the first datagram that verifies under a listed key whatever its epoch ().

section.name: Properties Provided
section.t: For a flow using manifest-ed25519-2, a receiver that follows delivers no datagram that the sender did not emit on that flow, under that key, in that epoch and flow generation (integrity and origin authenticity per datagram); admits each (digest, sequence) pair at most once and verifies each record once (replay, bounded within an epoch by sent at join and by the replay floor after the first verified record); and can detect deletion, loss and reordering within an epoch of the flow, since digest i of a record covers sequence = first_seq + i and the sequences of admitted datagrams are known. sequence and mseq restart at any value at an epoch change (, ), so where an epoch began is not known to a receiver, and where it ended is known only from a verified record whose flags bit 0 is set (); a deletion at either boundary is not a gap. That is the minimal standard of Section 2.3, "protection against replay, injection, and modification and the ability to detect deletion, loss, or reordering", a deleted datagram being a gap in the admitted sequences as a lost one is, and no mode of this document delivers an unauthenticated datagram (Section 2.4.4 of that document). Because every data datagram, repair symbols included, is admitted by its own digest before any use, an injected datagram cannot invalidate an object or a repair block and so force recovery, the amplification that Section 2.1 of that document describes; because a receiver delivers nothing it has not admitted, injected or modified traffic reaches no parser, decoder or renderer behind it, as Section 2.7.2 requires; and because a receiver can reject a flow its metadata does not authorize for the origin on whose behalf it acts (), it can unilaterally reject data the sender has not authorized for that page, the property Section 2.8.1 asks for. The pseudoheader in every digest and the prefix in every signature bind the datagrams to the flow and its generation, so an on-path adversary cannot swap the datagrams of two flows a receiver trusts, the example Section 2.5 of that document gives of what unbound delivery permits; that section asks for binding to a specific client request, and this document binds data to the flow the receiver chose to join and, where a profile derives ctx, to its application context, which is as far as a format with no return channel binds it.

The format provides no confidentiality: datagrams, records and keys are visible to every receiver and to the path, and the digests reveal whether two datagrams are identical. It provides no protection of availability ().

The format rests on the second-preimage resistance of H: an attacker that can find, for a digest in a verified record, another pseudoheader || payload with that digest has it admitted in place of the sender's datagram (); where the attacker can influence what the sender transmits it rests on collision resistance as well, and so does a profile that derives ctx with H (). A datagram whose content an attacker can predict lets it run that second-preimage search before the sender transmits the datagram, the offline attack on predictable packets that Section 8.1 describes; the pseudoheader adds nothing unpredictable, so the format relies on the strength of H alone against it rather than on unpredictable content. Collision difficulty is the digest anchor that Section 2.1 of names, and SHA-256 provides both properties at the full 256-bit output that requires. The Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry carries a Status field ( Section 9.4); a suite the registry marks deprecated no longer offers that assurance, and a sender that moves to another suite starts a new flow generation (). No receiver holds a secret: the verification keys are public, so a compromised or malicious receiver can forge nothing that another receiver admits, the asymmetric authentication of each content unit before any use that Section 2.4.4 of asks for; for a receiver that pins keys, the signing key is the flow's only long-term secret ().

section.name: Threat Model
section.t: This format protects against off-path and on-segment UDP injection, against corrupted or attacker-injected repair symbols, and against replay: a (record, datagrams) pair cannot be moved to another flow, flow generation, key or epoch (); an earlier epoch is rejected at join by minEpoch () and, on a receiver that pins keys, by the epoch floor kept with the pin, and after the first verified record by the current epoch, the previous epoch admitted until its grace period ends (); and within an epoch a receiver that checks freshness admits no window whose sent is more than 7 s + maxAuthDelayMs behind its clock, and, with the sender's clock within its 1 s bound and its own within 5 s, none emitted more than 13 s + maxAuthDelayMs before receipt, each plus any widening a profile specifies for a record on a path it adds (), so the verification budget cannot be spent with stale genuine records and the replay floor of takes over after the first verified record. A receiver that skips the freshness check can be fed the current epoch's earlier windows at join, and an injector that keeps its budget spent can hold it there. Clock skew beyond the 1 s and 5 s bounds of and costs availability where it makes the receiver's clock fast or the sender's slow: genuine records are dropped as stale. Skew the other way, a receiver clock slow or a sender clock fast by X in total, widens the replay window: the receiver admits at join windows older than the tolerance states by X, within the bounds as beyond them, and once X passes about 6 s it drops genuine records as future and admits only what an injector replays from that far back, so a receiver that cannot keep its clock within its bound does better to skip the freshness check, as allows, than to check against a clock it does not trust. An injector that can only replay what the multicast path has already delivered to the receiver meets the already-verified lookup and the replay floor of step 1. One that receives the records sooner, nearer the sender or over a faster path, forges nothing and still costs the receiver windows (step 1 of ): a copy that precedes the receiver's own by more than maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs is verified with pending entries that expire before the datagrams it covers arrive, the receiver's own copy then being dropped as already verified, so one record per window loses every window; a copy of mseq k that reaches the receiver before its own copy of mseq k - L, L above 64, raises highest_mseq to k, so the receiver's own copies of mseq k - L to k - 64 are dropped by the replay floor and those windows expire, one record per L - 63 windows losing all the others; and a copy of a new epoch's first record that precedes the receiver's own by more than maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs starts the previous epoch's grace period so early that it ends while that epoch's last records and twins are still to arrive. 64 windows pass in 64 / V seconds at the long-run ceiling of , under 8 ms at V = 8,248, so on a high-rate flow a small path advantage suffices; the verification budget does not bound this attack, which needs at most one record per window.

Metadata rewrite and key substitution are defended only for receivers that hold an out-of-band key pin. The digest algorithm is inside the signed record, so a rewrite can declare the flow unprotected, substitute keys or lower minEpoch; the pin catches the first two and the per-kid epoch floor kept with it () the third, except where a lowered minEpoch admits records of an earlier epoch signed with a still-listed kid: every earlier epoch at a receiver's first join under that kid, and at any later join the highest epoch verified under it, which the floor keeps rather than drops, and every later epoch in that kid's range, so a holder of a still-listed retired key signs fresh records of those epochs; either is admitted until a record of the current epoch is verified, and after that as the previous epoch (step 1 of ), so rotated-out keys SHOULD be removed promptly. A rewrite that raises minEpoch costs a receiver, pinned or not, that session's data and nothing more, since neither carries a metadata value past the session (). Rewriting any other parameter of the flow only makes genuine records fail the signature or ctx check, or resizes the verification budget, the hold queue and pending expiry (maxBitrate, maxAuthDelayMs, manifestTimerMs), which a receiver bounds by local policy (). A rewrite that redirects a receiver to another (S, G) is a join the receiver's metadata source authorized, and what it then receives verifies under the keys that metadata names or not at all; bounding the joins a receiver performs on behalf of one metadata source is a matter for the profile.

This format protects integrity, not availability. A forged record passes every check of step 1 of up to the signature, so each one spends a token of the verification budget: an attacker who sustains more than V records per second on the flow's port (about 1.3 Mbit/s of 164-octet records at V's floor, 10.8 Mbit/s at 8,248) takes a share of the budget proportional to its rate, and at several times that rate both copies of a window lose their tokens and the flow yields no data. The budget bounds the receiver's CPU; it does not raise the cost of this attack, and the record flood is not the cheapest availability attack on every protected flow: a data datagram that matches no pending entry is held until it expires (step 2 of ), and those expiries are loss to the application, so an injector that sustains, with the same access as the record flood, a given loss fraction does so for less than the V records per second the record flood needs wherever that fraction of the flow's packet rate is below it, as on every audio flow and most low-rate video; only evicting genuine datagrams, by overflowing the hold queue, needs the flow's bandwidth.
