On an SSM flow reached natively either flood must spoof S or be on path; on an ASM flow any host that can send to the group suffices, and so it does behind an AMT gateway, where a flood need only spoof the relay's address toward the gateway (). A datagram that expires from the hold queue is loss to the application; a held copy that step 1 drops because a record admitted another copy of the same datagram is not. A receiver SHOULD report records that the budget dropped for want of a token as loss as well, so that a sustained record flood is visible to the application rather than ending in silence.

Joining (S, G) delivers to the receiver's host every datagram the network forwards for (S, G), on every port, before any verification: multicast routing selects on addresses, not on UDP ports. Section 8.2 of describes what that does outside the receiver, a datagram injected into a subscribed group reaching an unrelated application on the host that listens on the unspecified address at another port, and recommends that senders list every flow they send in their metadata and that a firewall block multicast traffic to the unsecured ports of an (S, G) that carries secured traffic; a receiver that implements this document is not that application, but it pays for every datagram on port as states, so an attacker that can inject into the group spends the receiver's link before any check, and, where it sends as S (or as senderAddress on an ASM flow, ), its hashing budget as well; a datagram from any other source costs the one or two address comparisons of . This document bounds the price per datagram and the state: a datagram on port that passes the source and destination checks of and does not begin with "MHM2" is a data datagram and costs one hash and space in the hold queue, which is bounded in octets, until it expires, when it is dropped as unauthenticated, loss the application sees (step 2 of ). A datagram injected with "MHM2" at its start takes step 1 instead, where it is dropped before any cryptography or charged to the verification budget, exactly as it would be on a separate record port, and it never occupies the hold queue. Telling the two apart costs one four-octet comparison per datagram. The link capacity the injected traffic takes and the rate at which the receiver keeps hashing it are bounded by nothing here: a ceiling on the datagrams a receiver accepts from a joined group, counted before verification, and what it does when the ceiling is exceeded, belong to the profile's ingress ceiling (the browser profile, , drops datagrams above its ceiling before hashing, counts them and stays joined, unless the genuine datagrams among them trip its loss breaker).

A receiver that holds the metadata naming the successor key accepts the retired kid only below the successor's firstEpoch (), and records of the previous epoch only within its grace period, so for that receiver a key retired at an epoch boundary signs records admitted for at most maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs after the new epoch's first record is verified. An attacker that drops every record of the new epoch keeps the epoch before the change current at that receiver, and, holding the retired key, signs records that receiver admits until a record of the new epoch reaches it, the metadata removes the retired kid or the receiver is re-provisioned, minEpoch binding only a join. A receiver with older metadata is exposed to the retired key until it re-fetches, one metadata lifetime plus the 30 s re-fetch interval of at most, and a pinned receiver until it is re-provisioned.

Losing both copies of a window leaves at most 37 datagrams unauthenticated, which expire from the hold queue. Latency of authentication is bounded by maxAuthDelayMs. Digest i of a record covers sequence = first_seq + i, so deletion, loss and reordering within an epoch of a flow are detectable (the "ability to detect deletion, loss, or reordering" that Section 2.3 requires), and no mode of this document delivers an unauthenticated datagram (Section 2.4.4 of that document). A lost signed record is covered by its twin, at most maxAuthDelayMs / 2 later, so a held datagram waits at most that plus the burst that removed the record. The replay floor of 64 records below highest_mseq tolerates reordering of records on the flow's port by up to 63 windows, which is also the bound places on the twin's lag; a record reordered further is dropped, and its window is lost unless its other copy arrived in time.

A receiver that pins keys is exposed to nothing the metadata source can do beyond that session's data and the state that bounds by local policy: a minEpoch raise, a streamId change or a changed port or context source makes genuine records fail, maxBitrate, maxAuthDelayMs and manifestTimerMs resize its verification budget, hold queue and pending table, and a changed (S, G) is a join its metadata source authorized, but none of them lets it admit a datagram the sender did not emit; a receiver that does not pin is exposed to the metadata source as to the sender, which is why a profile fixes how the metadata is authenticated (, ).

The hold queue and its consume-on-admission rule descend from AMBI ( Section 3.2): a (digest, sequence) entry is consumed by one admission, and a copy of an admitted datagram that arrives while its digest is recorded as admitted, for maxAuthDelayMs after the admission, is dropped rather than held (steps 1 and 2 of ). The hold-down of that section, which keeps a consumed digest from being re-learned for the same sequence number from a later manifest, is replaced by the rule that a window's digests are inserted once, by the first verified copy of the record that carries them, its twin being dropped as already verified (step 1). The hold times are cut from the default hold times its Section 3.2.1 recommends, 2 s for data packets and 10 s for packet digests, to maxAuthDelayMs for datagrams (200 ms at the default) and maxAuthDelayMs + 2 x manifestTimerMs for digests (240 ms at the defaults).

section.name: Sender Responsibilities
section.t: For a receiver that pins keys, the signing key is the flow's only long-term secret: a sender that loses it to an attacker has given that attacker the flow until the key is removed from the metadata and every receiver has re-fetched or been re-provisioned, so a sender SHOULD keep a successor key published ahead of need () and remove a retired key promptly. The key that replaces a compromised one MUST carry a kid that no earlier key of the key set has carried: a receiver that pins keys keeps across sessions the highest epoch it has verified under each pinned kid (), an attacker holding the key can have raised that floor under the old kid past every epoch the sender will use (the newest key's range has no upper bound, ), and a replacement under the same kid would be dropped at join by every such receiver. For a receiver that takes its keys from the well-known document there is a second one, the private key of the TLS certificate for S, or whatever else authenticates the metadata channel a profile uses: its compromise lets an attacker publish keys of its own to every such receiver (), so the sender guards it as it guards the signing key. A sender MUST NOT reuse an epoch under a kid (), which requires it to keep the last epoch used under each kid across restarts, or to start under a new kid after a restart whose state is lost; an epoch reused under a kid reopens the windows of its first use to replay at a receiver that joins during the reuse: every one of them at a receiver that skips the freshness check of , and those emitted within the tolerance of step 1 of at one that checks it. A sender whose clock is off by more than the tolerance of makes its flow unverifiable to receivers that check freshness ().

section.name: The Trailer Scheme
section.t: ed25519-trailer-1 costs a receiver one signature verification per datagram, so every injected datagram that passes the replay window costs a verification: on a flow where any host can send to the group, or where S can be spoofed, the receiver's CPU is the attacker's to spend, which is why a receiver MAY refuse the scheme above 10 Mbit/s and why it is not mandatory (). A receiver MAY also bound the verifications it performs per second on such a flow by local policy, the limit on authentication checks per time unit that Section 7.1 recommends once the datagrams failing the check exceed a threshold, dropping genuine datagrams while the bound binds; the manifest scheme needs no such bound beyond the budget of step 1 of , since one verification admits up to 37 datagrams. The scheme's signed message binds S, G, port, epoch and seq but not streamId, and carries no domain-separation prefix: a datagram cannot be moved to another flow, epoch or position, and the scheme has no generation in the sense of , since a flow using it declares no streamId (); a sender restart is marked by epoch alone (). What keeps a datagram emitted before a restart out of the flow after it is epoch and seq in the signed message: the receiver drops a datagram of an epoch below the current one and one whose seq is below the window or already seen within it, and forbids a sender to reuse an epoch under a kid across restarts, so a replayed datagram of an earlier epoch is admitted only at join, or on the return to the join state of , before a datagram of a later epoch has verified (below); a sender that reused an epoch under a kid across restarts would let the earlier datagrams verify at the positions the window has not yet seen and, with a seq above the right edge, move the window past the genuine datagrams that follow, which the receiver then drops. A key used under any other scheme or protocol is not separated from that use. That is a known limitation of the scheme as defines it, which the author may change in a later revision of this document. The scheme carries no emission time and its metadata no minEpoch, so at join a receiver is exposed to replay of an earlier epoch under a still-listed key until it verifies a datagram of a later epoch, and to replay of the current epoch's earlier datagrams, each verifying as genuine, until a later datagram of that epoch verifies and moves the window's right edge past them, after which a replay 1024 or more below that edge, or already seen inside the window, is dropped (); removing retired keys promptly bounds the first exposure to the current key's epochs.

section.name: Trust in the Well-Known Document
section.t: The document is authenticated by the TLS certificate of the host at S, and nothing else: a certificate for S issued to an attacker, or a compromise of the host, lets the attacker substitute keys for every receiver that does not pin them, which covers. A receiver that verifies the certificate against the IP literal presents no server name in the handshake, so a host that serves several names must present the certificate for S to a client that sends none ( Section 7.4). The per-origin grant restricts which pages may join a flow, not who may fetch the document, which is public; a sender that does not want a flow's keys and parameters public does not publish them there. The fetch is itself a unicast connection to S, repeated every metadata lifetime and, at a receiver that re-fetches on a record with an unknown kid (), whenever such a record arrives, at most once per 30 s, that gives the operator of S the receiver's address, the time of each request, the origin of the page the receiver acts for, from the Origin header, and, where the page's referrer policy lets the fetch send the page's URL in a Referer header ( Section 10.1.3), that URL, and lets an on-path observer infer the subscription from traffic to a known S; this is the disclosure that Section 5.2 describes for a DORMS fetch, moved from the DORMS server to the source itself. A receiver that must not disclose this is provisioned out of band instead, or reaches S through a proxy that aggregates many receivers and does not terminate TLS, so that the certificate check against S still holds; this document specifies neither. A record with an unknown kid needs no key. Any host that can inject one datagram into the group therefore makes every receiver that re-fetches on such a record connect to S at once, a burst on S that grows with the audience and can recur every 30 s. By sending one, the sender learns which receivers are still joined at a moment it chooses, rather than once per metadata lifetime. A receiver that re-fetches only when the metadata lifetime expires, as the browser profile does and as every receiver does on a flow whose keys it pins (), takes part in neither. The document directs a receiver to join (S, G); a receiver that acts for a page bounds the joins it performs for that page, since a page could otherwise direct it at many groups and exhaust the network's join state, the attack that Section 4.5 describes.

section.name: Relationship to AMBI, ALTA, DORMS and MC_INTEGRITY
section.t: This appendix is informative. It places this document beside the work it descends from, in terms of what each document says; it makes no claim about what those documents' authors intend.

AMBI (). The digest of is the AMBI pseudoheader of its Section 3.4.2, with the same field layout, and the hold queue and consume-on-admission rule of are those of its Section 3.2. Two things differ. AMBI's Sections 3.4.2.1, 3.4.2.2, 3.4.2.6 and 3.4.2.7 take the addresses and ports from the packet on the wire; this document takes them from the flow's metadata, so that one digest verifies on whatever carrier delivers the datagram. AMBI's Section 3.3 manifest carries a stream identifier, a manifest sequence number, a first packet sequence number, an extensible TLV space (its Section 3.3.1.6) and digests, but no signature, and relies on its transport (Section 4.1: any authenticating transport; Sections 4.2 to 4.4: HTTPS, TLS and DTLS, all unicast) for authenticity; its Section 2.1.1 admits a protocol that signs manifests and delivers them over a multicast transport as a manifest delivery to be defined elsewhere, and this document's record is that delivery, defined as a separate signed record rather than an AMBI TLV so that it is a fixed layout, verified before any parsing and carried on the flow's own (S, G, port). AMBI's Sections 3.3.1.2 and 4.4 provide loss tolerance by overlapping successive manifests; this document uses non-overlapping windows and a byte-identical twin instead, so that a window's digests are inserted once and the replay floor and consume-once rule interact with nothing. AMBI names its hash algorithm in its YANG model; this document carries a Named Information Suite ID in the signed record.

ALTA (Asymmetric Loss-Tolerant Authentication, ). AMBI's Section 4.1 reserves a place for ALTA, which authenticates a multicast stream with an acyclic graph of message authentication codes (MACs) and regularly paced digital signatures. This document instead signs each window once and relies on the twin for loss: one signature per 37 datagrams, no MAC chain and no dependency between windows.

DORMS (). DORMS discovers a RESTCONF server for an (S, G) through reverse DNS (its Section 2.2) and serves YANG-modelled metadata from it, with a per-origin CORS grant that its Section 2.3.5 recommends and its Section 4.5 relies on against unauthorized pages. The well-known document of carries the same kind of metadata and the same grant from the source address itself under a certificate for that address, with no DNS hop, and treats a wildcard grant as no grant. DORMS's Section 2.2 lets a client with another way of finding a trusted server skip the DNS step, so a DORMS record remains one way to deliver the parameters of .

MC_INTEGRITY (). The multicast extension for QUIC carries a channel's packet hashes in MC_INTEGRITY frames sent from server to client (its Section 10.5) over an integrity-protected path other than that channel, either the client's unicast QUIC connection or another multicast channel whose packets an earlier frame verified, a Merkle tree whose root the unicast connection carries (its Section 4.5), each a hash of the encrypted channel packet (its Section 7.1), and names its hash algorithm from the same Named Information Hash Algorithm Registry this document uses. A receiver with no per-receiver QUIC connection, one behind an AMT relay, in a broadcast or in a browser without one, cannot anchor that tree, which is the case this document serves; the two carry different digests over different bytes and cannot share them, so they complement each other by deployment, not by format.

section.name: Change Log
section.t: This appendix is informative. It is to be removed before publication as an RFC.

ul.li: Records travel in band, on the flow's own (S, G, port) and interleaved with its data datagrams, and a receiver tells them from data by their first four octets, "MHM2", which no data datagram begins with (, ). The manifestPort parameter is removed, and the signature prefix of binds u16(port) in its place.
